de.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *de
Proto-Indo-European *-h₁
Proto-Indo-European *déh₁
Proto-Italic *dē
Latin dē
Dalmatian de
Inherited from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁.

glosses_en: blow, slap, smack, whack, knock, strike, thud
bot.etymology: Possibly from a derivative of Latin battuō, or alternatively of Germanic origin. Compare Italian botta, French botte.

aria.etymology: From Latin āērea or āēre, from āēr.

ci.etymology: From Latin quem. Compare Portuguese quem, Romanian cine, Spanish quien, Romansh che, Sardinian chíne.

glosses_en: mine; first-person masculine singular possessive pronoun
your; second-person masculine singular possessive pronoun
to.etymology: From Latin tuus. Compare Italian tuo, Romanian tău, Friulian to, French ton, Spanish tu.

plaza.etymology: From Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), clipping of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”).

vert.etymology: From Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis.

paraula.etymology: From Late Latin, from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”). Compare Spanish palabra, Italian parola.

pula.etymology: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pūbula, from Latin pūbes, or more likely from pulla, feminine of pullus. Compare Romanian pulă, Aromanian pulã, Catalan and Spanish polla.

sot.etymology: From Latin exsūctus (compare Italian asciutto, Venetan suto, Friulian sut, Spanish enjuto, Portuguese enxuto) or Latin suctus (compare Romanian supt).

fil.etymology: Ultimately from Latin fīlum. Judging by the /i/, presumably borrowed from Venetan or Italian filo.

ne.etymology: From Latin nec, neque. Compare Italian nè, Spanish, Catalan and French ni, Romanian nici.

noi.etymology: From Latin nōs. Compare Italian noi, French nous and Spanish nos.

voi.etymology: From Latin vōs. Compare Italian voi, Romanian voi, French vous.

aqua.etymology: From Latin aqua from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂. Compare Venetan àcua, Italian acqua.

farm.etymology: From Latin firmus. Compare Italian fermo.

da.etymology: From Latin de ab. Compare Italian da.

main.etymology: From Latin mēne, from mē. Compare Romanian mine.

ros.etymology: From Latin russus. Compare Occitan ros, French roux, Friulian ros.

vain.etymology: From Latin vīnum. Compare Istriot veîn.

cup.etymology: From Vulgar Latin capus, masculinization of Latin caput. Compare Italian capo, Romanian cap, Spanish cabo.

catur.etymology: Ultimately from Latin captāre, possibly via Venetan catar on both semantic grounds (both mean 'find') and phonological (Dalmatian lacks the expected /p/; cf. sapto < Latin septem).

fin.etymology: From Latin faenum. Compare Italian fieno, Romanian fân, Friulian fen, Romansh fain, French foin, Portuguese feno, Spanish heno. Alternative form also possibly through a Venetan intermediate as a loan word.

baud.etymology: From Latin vōx, vocem, possibly influenced by vōtum.

le.etymology: From Latin illae, nominative feminine plural of ille.

blanc.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin blancus, perhaps via Old Venetan blanco. Compare also Italian bianco.

trist.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis.

fen.etymology: From Latin fīnitus. Compare Italian fino.

tot.etymology: From Latin tōtus. Compare Romanian, Romansh, Occitan, and Catalan tot, Italian tutto, French tout, Spanish and Portuguese todo.

bin.etymology: From Latin bene. Compare Romanian bine, Italian bene, Spanish bien, French bien.

tun.etymology: From Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos). Compare Italian tuono, Friulian ton, Catalan tro, Romansh tun, tung, Romanian tun, tunet, Spanish trueno.

col.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cu illu, contracted from the accusative of Vulgar Latin *eccum ille. Compare Italian quello, Romanian acel, Old French cil, Spanish aquel.

azul.etymology: From Medieval Latin lazulum, from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward), from Classical Persian لَاجَوَرْد (lājaward).

mesu.etymology: From a cross of Latin mēnsus (“measured, distributed”) and medius (“middle, half”). Like Sardinian mesu and perhaps Venetan miso; unlike Italian mezzo and Romanian miez.

cil.etymology: From Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-. Compare Istriot sil.

jo.etymology: From Latin ubi. Compare Romanian iuo, Italian ove, French où, Old Spanish o.

civet.etymology: Compare Italian civetta, Romansh tschuetta, French chouette.

dais.etymology: From Latin dē(n)sus. Compare Italian denso, Romanian des.

lac.etymology: From Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).

limp.etymology: From a derivative of Latin lampas. Compare Italian lampo.

dai.etymology: Inherited from Classical Latin diēs. Compare Istriot dèi, Venetan dì and archaic Italian dì, Romanian zi.

plain.etymology: From Latin plēnus. Compare Italian pieno, Romansh plain, Romanian plin, French plein.

mil.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.

glosses_en: white (referring exclusively to fabric or wool)
blank.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan bianco. Interestingly, both /bl-/ and /bj-/ are recorded in Udina's speech. According to Bartoli, the /l/ is secondary. The form blanco is attested in Venetan until the second half of the 14th century, but Venetian con

buc.etymology: Possibly from a Latin root buculus (“young bull, ox, steer”). Compare French bugle, beugle.

zer.etymology: Inherited from Latin īre. The present and subjunctive forms are based on Latin vādere.

ri.etymology: From Latin reus. Compare Italian rio, Romanian rău.

bosca.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *bauscia or *baucia, of Germanic origin. Compare Italian bugia, Friulian bausie, Occitan bauzia, bauza, Old French boisie, Sardinian bigía, busia.

mais.etymology: From Latin mē(n)sis. Compare French mois, Italian mese, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.

glas.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/-a, from Latin glaciēs.

anca.etymology: From Latin hanc hodie. Compare Istriot anca, Venetan anca, Italian anche, Friulian ancje, Occitan ancui.

vaca.etymology: From Latin vacca (“cow”). Compare Italian vacca, Spanish vaca.

sait.etymology: From Latin sitis. Compare Italian and Romanian sete, Romansch said.

busca.etymology: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin form of Latin bōs, bovem + feminine of -esco. Compare bu (“ox”).

glosses_en: a female given name from Hebrew, equivalent to English Eve

vai.etymology: From Latin hodie. Compare Friulian vuê.

venja.etymology: From Latin vīnea. Compare Italian vigna, Portuguese vinha, Spanish viña, French vigne, Romanian vie.

pur.etymology: From Latin pāret, third person singular present active indicative of pareō.

masa.etymology: From Late Latin missa, from Latin missum < mittō.

drat.etymology: From Late Latin drictus, from Latin dīrēctus.

samur.etymology: From Late Latin sagmarius; compare Latin sagma, Italian somaro, Istriot samèri.

saur.etymology: From Latin soror, with the variant form seraur deriving from the Latin accusative form sorōrem. Compare Romanian soră, suroră, sor, Italian suora, Old Italian suoro, French soeur, Old Spanish seror, Spanish sor, Friulian sûr, Romansch sora,

coser.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *cosīre < *cōsere, from Latin cōnsuere.

tara.etymology: From Latin terra. Compare Italian and Portuguese terra, Romansh terra, tiara, teara, Romanian țară, Spanish tierra, French terre.

vaina.etymology: From Latin vēna. Compare Romansh avaina, Italian vena, Romanian vână, French veine.

doi.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *duī, from duo. Compare Romanian and Friulian doi, Italian due, French deux.

cris.etymology: From Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.

lois.etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *liseus or *lisius, perhaps from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Compare Italian liscio, Portuguese and Spanish liso, Catalan llis, Sicilian lisciu, Friulian lis, Romansh glisch.

bura.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin boreas < Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās). Compare Italian borea, Romanian bură, Venetan bura.

glosses_en: mine; first-person feminine singular possessive pronoun
maja.etymology: From Latin mea, feminine of meus.

jala.etymology: From Latin illa, feminine of ille. Compare Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan ella, French elle, Romanian ea.

mur.etymology: From Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.

dona.etymology: From Latin domina. Compare Catalan dona, Italian donna, Romanian doamnă.

jorden.etymology: From Latin ōrdō, ōrdinem, possibly through Italian ordine.

fiar.etymology: From Latin ferrum. Compare Italian ferro, Romanian and Romansh fier, Friulian fiêr, French fer, Sardinian ferru, Spanish hierro.

glosses_en: your; second-person feminine singular possessive pronoun
toa.etymology: From Latin tua, feminine of tuus.

nina.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ninna, a nursery or infantile word.

stal.etymology: Possibly from Latin stilos (“stake”); compare also Italian stollo, possibly of Germanic origin.

buna.etymology: From Latin bonus. Compare Romanian bună.

rau.etymology: From Latin reus. Compare Italian rio, Romanian rău.

mut.etymology: From Latin modo. Compare regional Italian mo, compare Romanian măi.

glosses_en: cat (Felis silvestris catus, a domesticated feline commonly kept as a house pet)

dri.etymology: From Latin dē retrō. Compare Italian dietro, French derrière, and Venetan drio.

rus.etymology: From Latin radius. Compare Italian raggio, Romanian rază.

rait.etymology: From Latin rēte. Compare Italian rete, Friulian rêt, Romansh rait.

bluta.etymology: From Latin oblāta. Compare French oublie.

calco.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum ille followed by Latin qui.

cauda.etymology: From Latin cauda, either directly (with preservation of /au̯/) or, more likely, via Vulgar Latin cōda (the source of all other Romance forms), with /'oː/ > /au̯/; cf. Latin nōmen > Dalmatian naum.

jali.etymology: From Latin illī, nominative masculine plural of ille.

comparer.etymology: From Latin compareo, comparere. Compare Italian comparire.

jale.etymology: From Latin illae, nominative feminine plural of ille.

maisa.etymology: From Vulgar Latin mēsa, from Latin mēnsa. Compare Romansh maisa, Italian mensa, Romanian masă, Spanish mesa.

glosses_en: having the color of human skin
drap.etymology: From Late Latin drappus, drappum (“cloth”); compare Italian drappo, French drap.

quaranta.etymology: From Late Latin quarranta, from Latin quadrāgintā, possibly via Italian quaranta.

sputa.etymology: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē).

trok.etymology: Borrowed from South Slavic, whence Serbo-Croatian otrȍk and Slovene otrȍk (“child, youngster”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *otròkъ.

maur.etymology: From Latin maior, maiōrem. Compare also Romanian mare (“large”).

ju.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆. Cognate with Sicilian ju.

glosses_en: our; first-person feminine plural possessive pronoun
nuestra.etymology: From Latin nostra, feminine of noster.

cual.etymology: From Latin collum. Compare Italian collo, Spanish cuello.

nai.etymology: From Latin nix, nivem. Compare Romanian nea, Italian neve, Romansh naiv, Catalan neu.

duas.etymology: From Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum.

diaul.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

jamo.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ad modo. Compare Romanian amu, Aromanian amo, acmo.

tuota.etymology: From Latin tata. Compare Romanian tată.

paina.etymology: From Latin penna and pinna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).

coisa.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. Compare Italian così, Istriot cussèi, Venetan cusì, Friulian cussì.

saltur.etymology: From saltāre. Compare French sauter, Italian saltare, Portuguese saltar, Spanish saltar.

glosses_en: your second-person masculine plural possessive determiner
your; second-person feminine plural possessive pronoun
vestra.etymology: From Latin vostra, feminine of voster.

čama.etymology: From Latin cyma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma).

glosses_en: Four attached little loaves of bread; row of loaves attached by thin kissing crust.
turta.etymology: From Latin turta. Thought to derive from tŏrta f (“twisted”), but this is problematic.

caval.etymology: From Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”).

puant.etymology: From Latin pontem, accusative singular of pōns. Compare Friulian puint, Spanish puente.

jongla.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ungla, from Latin ungula.

lavorar.etymology: From Latin laborāre. Compare Italian lavorare.

sabata.etymology: From Latin sabbata, from sabbatum. Cognate with Romanian sâmbătă, Friulian sabide, Ladin sabeda, Romansh sonda, Italian sabato, French samedi, Spanish sábado.

fiata.etymology: Probably from the feminine of a Vulgar Latin *fictus < Latin fissus, past participle of findere. Compare Italian fetta, Spanish and Portuguese fita, Sardinian and Sicilian fitta.

falur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallēre. Compare Italian fallare.

saita.etymology: From Latin seta < saeta. Compare Italian seta, Romansh saida, Spanish seda.

glosses_en: Dalmatia (a historical region of Croatia, on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea)
Dalmatia (a province of the Roman Empire)

paira.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pira (taken as a feminine singular), from the plural of Latin pirum. Compare Italian, Spanish pera, Romanian pară, French poire, Romansch pair, paira.

duag.etymology: From Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ). Compare Italian doga, Romanian doagă, French douve.

pial.etymology: From Latin pellis, pellem. Compare Italian pelle, Portuguese pele, Friulian and Spanish piel, Romanian piele.

agost.etymology: From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus.

mirte.etymology: From Latin Martis dīēs, variant of dīēs Martis.

batar.etymology: Inherited from Latin battere, from earlier battuere.

paradais.etymology: From Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos).

tacla.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tegla, from Latin tēgula. Compare Venetan técia, Friulian tecje, Italian teglia, tegghia.

muas.etymology: From a derivative of Latin marceō (“wither”).

jarma.etymology: From Latin arma, possibly through Italian arma. Cognate with Sicilian arma.

scol.etymology: From Latin schola (“school”), from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ). Compare Italian scuola, Spanish escuela, Portuguese escola, and French école.

braz.etymology: From Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn). Compare Italian braccio, Romanian braț, Spanish brazo, French bras.

jal.etymology: From Latin ille. Compare Romanian el, Italian egli, French il, Sicilian iḍḍu, Spanish él.

avoit.etymology: Past participle of avar. From Vulgar Latin *habūtus, replacing Classical Latin habitus.

cic.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin qualis que. Compare Italian qualcuno, French quelque, Spanish cualque.

faid.etymology: From Latin fidem. Compare Friulian fede.

brusc.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *bruscus, from Latin rūscus or rūscum. Compare Catalan brusc, Italian brusco, French brusque, Spanish brusco.

chis.etymology: From Latin cāseus. Compare Italian cacio, Romanian caș, Spanish queso.

amia.etymology: From Latin amita. Compare Venetan àmia.

destruar.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *dēexcitāre, from Latin dē + excitāre. Compare Italian destare. Compare also Romanian deștepta.

lotum.etymology: From Latin laetāmen < laetus (“happy, rich, also later fertile”). Compare Italian and Spanish letame.

fure.etymology: From Latin foras or forīs . Compare Italian fuori.

cincto.etymology: Possibly borrowed from Vulgar Latin cinctus, re-formed from Latin quintus.

oracla.etymology: Inherited from Latin ōricula, variant of auricula.

glosses_en: your second-person masculine plural possessive pronoun

saira.etymology: From Late Latin sēra, from ellipsis of Latin sēra dies, from sērus (“late”). Compare Italian sera, Romanian seară, French soir, Romansch saira.

miur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mēiāre, from Latin mēiere. Compare Spanish mear, Portuguese mijar.

capula.etymology: From Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

frete.etymology: From Latin frīctae, plural of frīcta, feminine of frīctus.

scior.etymology: From Latin obscūrus. Compare Italian scuro.

pauc.etymology: From Latin paucus. Compare Italian and Spanish poco, Romansch and Occitan pauc, Friulian pôc, Catalan poc, Portuguese pouco.

plui.etymology: From Latin *plagium, ultimately from Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios). Compare Romanian plai. Compare plagia, whence came Italian spiaggia, piaggia, French plage, Spanish playa, Portuguese praia.

vindre.etymology: From Latin Veneris diēs < diēs Veneris.

vun.etymology: Ultimately from Latin avēna; cf. Italian avena. Compare also Venetan véna, Friulian vene, French avoine.

camain.etymology: From Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμινος (káminos). Compare Istriot cameîn, Venetan camin, Italian camino.

glosses_en: to favour, promote, encourage, prefer, further, support

siansa.etymology: Compare Italian senza, Istriot and Venetan sensa. Probably ultimately from Latin absentia.

cauc.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *hocce, from Latin hoc. Compare Romanian încoace, acoace, auace.

abrasur.etymology: Probably from braz (“arm”), or from a Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o. Compare Italian abbracciare, Sicilian abbrazzari.

agaun.etymology: Compare Italian agone (“shad”) (an augmentative form of ago (“needle”)) and Venetan agon.

alaura.etymology: From Latin ad illam hōram (“at that hour”). Compare Italian allora, French alors.

alegr.etymology: From Latin alacer, alacrem. Compare Italian allegro and Venetan aliegro, however.

a lič.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin ad + latus. Compare Italian allato, lato, Romanian alături, Old French lez.

alzur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).

ancusene.etymology: From Latin incus, incudem (through a Vulgar Latin root *incudinem). Compare Venetan ancùxene, Italian incudine.

aninč.etymology: From Late Latin in ante, from Latin in + ante.

pascu.etymology: From Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).

ascianz.etymology: From Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion). Compare Italian assenzio.

bajur.etymology: Possibly from Latin baubari. Compare Italian abbaiare, French aboyer, Friulian bajâ, Venetan bajar, bagiar.

basalca.etymology: From Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ).

blasmur.etymology: Ultimately or directly from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre).

boscur.etymology: From a derivative of Late Latin boscus, of Germanic origin. Compare Italian bosco, Spanish bosque.

botaiga.etymology: From Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “repository”).

botaila.etymology: Ultimately from Late Latin butticula, probably via a northern Italian derivative of Old French boteille.

botaun.etymology: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *botonus or *bottonem. Compare Italian bottone, French bouton, Spanish botón, Romansh buttun, Sardinian butòne.

glosses_en: to throw away, trash, chuck, dump
botur.etymology: Probably ultimately of Germanic origin. Compare Italian buttare, French bouter, Spanish botar.

braina.etymology: Cf. Italian briglia, French bride, Spanish brida.

bramur.etymology:
Probably ultimately of Germanic origin; see Italian bramire.
Compare Italian bramare, Spanish bramar, Spanish bramer, also Sardinian abbramíre. Another possibility may be a Latin root *peramō < per + amō.

broin.etymology: From Medieval Latin brūnus (“brown, brunet”) (whence also Spanish bruno, French brun), from Proto-West Germanic *brūn, from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz (“brown”).

bruf.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus, or from bravium. Compare Italian, Spanish, Portuguese bravo, French brave, Occitan brau, Sardinian bràvu, Romansch brav.

bruod.etymology: From Late Latin brodium, of ultimately Germanic origin (compare Italian brodo).

brusur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *brusiāre, itself possibly from a form *per-ust(ul)āre < Latin per + ustulāre (compare perurere). Compare Italian bruciare, French brûler, Occitan bruslar, buizar, Romansh brischar.

bualp.etymology: From Latin vulpēs, vulpem. Compare Istriot bulpo, Venetan bolp, volp, bolpe, Friulian bolp, Ladin volp, Romansh vulp, vualp, Italian volpe.

buarca.etymology: From Late Latin barca, probably from Latin baris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris), itself probably of Egyptian origin.

buarsa.etymology: From Late Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa).

buasc.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

buast.etymology: Probably from Italian busto, from Latin būstum.

buola.etymology: Of Germanic origin. Compare Italian palla, Occitan bala, French balle.

buonda.etymology: Of Germanic origin. Compare Spanish and Italian banda, French bande.

butir.etymology: From Latin būtȳrum < Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron).

cadar.etymology: From Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

cadrial.etymology: From a diminutive of Latin quadrus, possibly a Vulgar Latin root *quadrellus. Compare Italian quadrello, French carreau, Spanish cuadrillo.

calčaina.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *calcīna, from Latin calx. Compare Italian calcina, Old French chaucine.

camaisa.etymology: From Late Latin camisia. Compare Italian camicia, Romanian cămașă, Spanish camisa.

campanaid.etymology: From a derivative of Late Latin campāna. Compare Italian campanile.

canaisa.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *cinisia, from Latin cinis. Compare Italian cinigia, Portuguese cinza, Romanian cenușă, Spanish ceniza.

canapial.etymology: From a derivative of Vulgar Latin *canapus, *canapis, Late Latin canapa, from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis).

cand.etymology: From Latin quando. Compare Romanian când, Italian quando, Portuguese quando, French quand.

capei.etymology: From Latin capilli, plural of capillus. Compare Italian capelli.

capraina.etymology: From a derivative of Latin capra.

carnual.etymology: From Latin carnālis. Compare Portuguese carneiro, Spanish carnero.

carviale.etymology: From Latin cerebellum. Compare Italian cervello, French cerveau.

glosses_en: to have supper, have a meal, dine, eat

cluf.etymology: From Latin clāvis, clāvem. Compare French clef.

codial.etymology: From a diminutive of Latin coda.

comnut.etymology: From Latin cōgnātus. Compare Romanian cumnat, Italian cognato.

cončaro.etymology: From Latin conquaerere, variant of conquirō.

conmaic.etymology: From Latin cum mēcum. Compare Italian meco (Old Italian conmeco), Portuguese comigo, Spanish conmigo.

cortial.etymology: From Latin cultellus. Compare Istriot curtielo, Venetan cortèƚo.

cosuol.etymology: From Late Latin casālis (“domestic,belonging to the house”) or casāle (“country house, farm”), ultimately from Latin casa. Compare Italian casale, Old French chesal, Spanish casal.

cratoire.etymology: From Late Latin creātūrae, plural of creātūra, from Latin creō. Compare Italian creatura, Spanish criatura.

cuarno.etymology: From Latin cornu. Compare Istriot cuorno, Italian corno, Romanian corn, Friulian cuar, Spanish cuerno.

cuasta.etymology: From Latin costa. Compare Italian costa, Romanian coastă, Friulian cueste, Spanish cuesta.

čaico.etymology: Probably from a compound of Vulgar Latin *hicce (< Latin hīc) or of quī or que. Compare Romanian aici, aci, acice, Italian ci, qui, Old Italian quici.

čauca.etymology: Compare Italian chioccia, Spanish clueca, Portuguese choca.

čedur.etymology: Borrowed from Italian cedere, itself borrowed from Latin cēdere.

čertjoin.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *certānus, derived from Latin certus.

ciant.etymology: From Latin centum, perhaps borrowed via Italian, considering the palatalization before Latin /ē/.

cič.etymology: From Latin cicer. Compare Italian cece.

cir.etymology: From Latin cereum. Compare Italian cero.

circol.etymology: Ultimately from Latin circulus, presumably borrowed through Italian circolo.

cistierna.etymology: From Latin cisterna. Compare Italian cisterna, Friulian cistierne, Istriot zustierna.

čuarv.etymology: Uncertain. Compare Italian guercio, Occitan guer, guerle, Spanish guercho, Catalan guerxo and Ladin guersch.

dapú.etymology: From Latin de post. Compare Istriot duopo, Venetan dapò, Italian dopo, Romanian după, Sicilian dopu, Friulian daspò, French depuis.

dauc.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *dux (“source, spring”). Compare Italian dogaia, Old French doiz, Old Spanish aduz.

debeta.etymology: Ultimately from Latin debitum, probably through the plural form debita. Compare Italian debito, Spanish deuda, Portuguese dívida, French dette.

débol.etymology: From Latin debilis. Compare Latin debole, Istriot dibalo, dibulo, Venetan debol.

defuant.etymology: From Latin defunctus. Compare Italian defunto.

dementicur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *dismenticāre, perhaps via Italian dimenticare.

demun.etymology: From Latin daemon, from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn).

denacle.etymology: From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”).

denj.etymology: From Latin dignus. Compare Italian degno.

dentul.etymology: From Medieval Latin or Late Latin dentālis, derived from Latin dēns (“tooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts.

depentaur.etymology: Derived from the verb depiandro, or from the form pentaur, and influenced by the verb with the prefix de-. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pinctor, pinctōrem, from Latin pictor. Cf. French peintre, Spanish pintor.

depotur.etymology: From Latin dēputāre. Compare Italian deputare.

depotut.etymology: From the past participle of depotur. Compare Italian deputato.

desmun.etymology: From Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”), possibly via Vulgar Latin *dē ipsō māne.

dessendiansia.etymology: From dessendro. Compare Latin descendentia. Compare Italian discendenza.

desirur.etymology: From Latin dēsīderāre. Compare French désirer, Occitan desirar, Italian desiderare.

despreziur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *dispretiō. Compare Italian disprezzare, Occitan and Portuguese desprezar, Spanish despreciar.

juv.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum.

destinur.etymology: From Latin dēstinō, dēstināre, probably borrowed; cf. Italian destinare.

dezun.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin iēiūnium. Compare Italian digiuno, Catalan dejuni.

diant.etymology: From Latin dēns, dentem. Compare Italian dente, Portuguese dente, Romanian dinte, Friulian dint, Venetan dénte, French dent, Spanish diente.

discopiart.etymology: From Late Latin discoopertus, from Latin dis- + coopertus.

discualz.etymology: From Latin discalceātus < discalceō. Compare Romanian desculț, Friulian discolç, Italian scalzo, Spanish descalzo, Portuguese descalço, Sardinian caltzadu.

glosses_en: speech, talk, discourse, address, delivery, remark, chat
discuars.etymology: From Late Latin discursus, from Latin discurrō.

glosses_en: to have lunch, eat lunch, lunch
disnur.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre, from disieiūnāre (“to break the fast”), from Late Latin dis- + iēiūnō (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus. Compare Old French disner (modern dîner); compare also déjeuner, Spanish desayunar.

dispiat.etymology: From Latin despectus. Compare Italian dispetto.

distruzar.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

domandur.etymology: From Latin demandāre. Compare Italian domandare, Venetan domandar.

domienca.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”). Compare Italian domenica.

doperur.etymology: From Late Latin adoperāre, from Latin ad + operāre. Compare Italian adoperare.

dotuar.etymology: Ultimately from Latin doctor. Compare Italian dottore.

dovar.etymology: From Latin dēbēre. Compare Italian dovere, French devoir.

dramur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre (“strip off, cut away branches”), from Latin rāmus. Compare Romanian dărâma, Italian diramare, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.

drante.etymology: From Latin de + intro. Compare Istriot drento, Venetan drénto, Italian, Spanish dentro.

drecno.etymology: From Latin ricinus. Compare Spanish rezno.

driaz.etymology: From Vulgar Latin trichia, from Ancient Greek τριχία (trikhía). Compare Italian treccia/trezza, Spanish trenza, French tresse, Portuguese trança.

du andú.etymology: From Latin dē unde. Compare Spanish donde, Portuguese donde.

duanc.etymology: From Vulgar Latin dunc. Compare French donc, Venetan donca.

duauta.etymology: From Latin dōs, dotem. Compare Italian dota, dote.

dulsassa.etymology: Cf. dolc. Compare Italian dolcezza, Romanian dulceață.

encontrur.etymology: From Latin in contrā. Compare Italian incontrare, Old French encontrer, Spanish and Portuguese encontrar.

glosses_en: to fatten, get/grow fat, gain weight
engrassur.etymology: From a derivative of Latin crassus. Compare Spanish engrasar, Italian ingrassare, French engraisser, Portuguese engraxar, Romanian îngrășa.

glosses_en: matter, business, affair, concern, issue, job
facianda.etymology: From Latin facienda. Compare Italian faccenda.

faguor.etymology: From a derivative of Latin fagus. Compare Italian faggio, Venetan fagaro, faghèr, faghèra, Friulian faiâr.

faica.etymology: Ultimately from Latin fīcus through a feminine Vulgar Latin form *fīca. Compare Italian fica, Catalan and Catalan fica, Aromanian hicã.

famalja.etymology: From Latin familia. Compare Italian and Romansh famiglia, Aromanian fumealje, Friulian famee, Venetan faméja.

fasul.etymology: From Latin phaseolus, probably from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos).

fataica.etymology: From faticur. Compare Italian fatica, Istriot fadeîga.

abandonur.etymology: Compare Italian abbandonare, compare also Friulian bandonâ, Romansch bandunar.

fazuol.etymology: Probably borrowed from Italian fazzuolo. Or, less likely from Venetan fasoło.

fecuat.etymology: From Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver”).

fejustro.etymology: From Late Latin fīliaster, fīliastrum, from Latin fīlius.

fial.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.

fiasta.etymology: From Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstum. Compare Friulian fieste, Romansh fiasta, Spanish fiesta.

fichiera.etymology: From Latin fīcāria. Compare Catalan figuera, French figuier, Portuguese figueira, Spanish higuera.

glosses_en: to stop, arrest, staunch, halt, end
fermur.etymology: From Latin firmō; compare Italian fermare.

finiastra.etymology: From Latin fenestra. Compare Italian finestra, Romanian fereastră, French fenêtre.

fiaur.etymology: Ultimately from Latin flōrem. The /j/ is unexpected for an inherited Dalmatian word and may indicate that this form was influenced by Venetan fior.

fiorain.etymology: Diminutive of fiaur. Compare Italian fiorino.

formaica.etymology: From Latin formīca. Compare Dalmatian furmeîga, Venetan formìga.

forsaura.etymology: From Late Latin frixōria (“frying-pan”), from Latin frigere (“fry”).

frazial.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fragellum, by dissimilation from Latin flagellum.

fregur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *frigāre, from Latin frīgere.

fualja.etymology: From Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium. Compare Italian foglia, Romanian foaie, Friulian fuee, Venetan fogia, French feuille, Portuguese folha, Catalan fulla.

fuart.etymology: From Latin fortis, fortem. Compare Italian forte, Romanian foarte, Spanish fuerte, French and Catalan fort, Friulian fuart.

fuc.etymology: From Latin focus. Compare Italian fuoco, Friulian fûc, Romanian and Catalan foc, French feu, Spanish fuego, Portuguese fogo, Occitan fuòc.

gelut.etymology: From Latin gelātus. Compare Italian gelato, gelata, French gelée, Spanish helado, helada, Portuguese geada, Catalan gelat, gelada.

golaus.etymology: From Latin gulōsus. Compare Italian and Spanish goloso.

inamiant.etymology: Ultimately from Latin mens. Compare Romanian aminti, aduce a minte, Old Italian ammentare, Spanish mentar, Portuguese amentar.

inflorer.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *inflōrīre < inflōrēscere, from Latin flōrēscere. Compare Romanian înflori, Italian fiorire, infiorare.

inghiastro.etymology: From Late Latin encaustum, from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston). Compare Italian inchiostro, French encre.

intric.etymology: From Latin integer, integrum. Compare Romanian întreg, Italian intero, French entier, Spanish entero.

saite.etymology: Ultimately from forms of Latin sum.

inviarno.etymology: From Late Latin hībernum. For the added nasal in the first syllable, cf. Italian inverno, etc.

jauca.etymology: From Late Latin auca, contraction of *avica < Latin avis (“bird”).

lačar.etymology: From Latin lacerta. Compare Italian lucertola, Sicilian lucerta, French lézard.

lampur.etymology: From a derivative of Latin lampas. Compare Italian lampeggiare, lampare, Spanish relampaguear, Portuguese lampejar.

luang.etymology: From Latin longus. Compare Italian lungo, luongo, Romanian lung, Spanish luengo, French long.

luc.etymology: From Latin illoc. Compare Romanian acolo, Old Italian loco, Old French iluec.

luntun.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longē. Compare Italian lontano, French lointain, Sicilian luntanu, Friulian and Romansch lontan.

macnur.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Compare Venetan masnar~maxenar, Friulian masanâ, Italian macinare.

mančur.etymology: From Latin mandūcāre, presumably borrowed via Italian mangiare, itself borrowed from Old French mangier. Compare also Romanian mânca.

manzula.etymology: From the feminine of Latin manuciolus (“small bundle”).

marianda.etymology: From Latin merenda. Compare Istriot and Venetan marenda, Italian merenda, Romanian merinde, Spanish merienda.

medco.etymology: From Latin medicus. Compare Italian medico, Catalan metge.

mejatoira.etymology: Ultimately from the Latin verb meiō, probably with a derivative of the suffix -tura. Compare the Dalmatian verb miur (“to urinate”).

menur.etymology: From Latin mināre, collateral form of minārī. Compare Friulian menâ.

mescur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mixticāre, derived from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Compare Italian mesticare, Romanian (a)mesteca.

miarda.etymology: From Latin merda. Compare Italian merda, Spanish mierda, Friulian mierde, Romansh merda, miarda.

miarla.etymology: From Latin merula. Compare Romanian mierlă, Italian merla, Spanish mierla.

misedma.etymology: From Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin media hebdomas < Latin media (“middle”) + hebdomas (“week”). Compare archaic/regional Italian mezzedima (“Wednesday”), Romansh mesemna (“Wednesday”).

tinir.etymology: From a derivative of Late Latin tīnum, from Latin tīna (“wine-vessel”). Compare Spanish and Italian tino.

monaita.etymology: From Latin monēta. Compare Italian moneta, Romansh munaida.

muart.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mortu(s), from Latin mortuus. Compare Italian morto, Romanian mort, Spanish muerto, French and Catalan mort, Friulian muart, Romansch miert.

mucna.etymology: Inherited from Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Compare Italian macina.

muncial.etymology: From Late Latin monticellus, derivative of Latin mons. Compare Romanian muncel, Italian monticello, moncello, French monceau, Spanish montecillo.

nascoit.etymology: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *nāscūtus, from Latin nāscor. Compare Romanian născut, Catalan and Occitan nascut, Friulian nassût.

nauc.etymology: From Latin nux, nucem. Compare Romanian nuc, nucă, Italian noce, French noix, Spanish nuez.

naul.etymology: Probably from Latin avulus (“grand-daddy”), diminutive of avus. Compare Italian avolo.

nenčoin.etymology: From Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”).

niapta.etymology: From Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis.

ninapta.etymology: From a derivative of Latin nupta (“bride”). Possibly influenced by Proto-Slavic *nevěsta of the same meaning. Compare Romanian nevastă.

nochiera.etymology: From Late Latin (arbor) nucāria, from nucārius < nux (“nut”). Compare Spanish noguera, Portuguese nogueira, French noyer, Catalan noguera, Occitan noguièr.

nolja.etymology: From Latin nūlla, feminine of nūllus. Compare Italian nulla.

glosses_en: our first-person masculine plural possessive pronoun

ourata.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *orāta, from Latin aurāta. Compare Italian orata; compare also Spanish dorado, dorada, Portuguese dourado, dourada, French daurade.

paserain.etymology: From a derivative of Latin passer, passerem. Compare Italian passero, Romanian pasăre, Spanish pájaro, Portuguese pássaro.

pasnur.etymology: From Latin pastinō. Compare Italian pastinare, Old French pasner.

pecla.etymology: From Late Latin picula, diminutive of Latin pix. Compare Italian pegola, Romanian păcură.

pedlo.etymology: Probably formed from a Latin root *picc-. Compare Romanian pic, Italian piccolo, Italian piccino.

pedoclo.etymology: From Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus, from pēdis.

percó.etymology: From Latin per quod. Compare Italian perché.

pernaica.etymology: From Latin perdīcem, which was borrowed from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix). For the /d/ > /n/, compare Italian pernice.

pescatoira.etymology: From a derivative of Latin pesculum, from pessulum, with the suffix -atura.

pesunt.etymology: From Latin pēnsāns, present participle of pēnsō. Compare Italian pesante. Doublet of pesaint.

piandro.etymology: From Latin pingō. Compare French peindre.

piardro.etymology: From Latin perdere. Compare Romanian pierde, Italian perdere, Spanish perder, French perdre, Friulian pierdi, Romansh perder, piarder.

pitra.etymology: From Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra).

pizaraul.etymology: Possibly from a deriviative of a Vulgar Latin *pitsarolius root *pits ("point"), with the diminutive -ariolus, or related to Italian pizza.

pjancura.etymology: Borrowed from an Italian derivative of Late Latin planca, from plancus.

poluastro.etymology: From a derivative of Latin pullastra, from pullus. Compare Italian pollastro, Catalan pollastre.

potar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

potuor.etymology: From Latin putāre (“clean, cleanse”). Compare Italian potare, Spanish podar.

priast.etymology: From Late Latin praestus. Compare Italian presto.

prinz.etymology: From Latin prandium. Compare Romanian prânz, Italian pranzo.

puarc.etymology: From Latin porcus. Compare Italian porco, Spanish puerco, Romanian porc.

puarta.etymology: From Latin porta. Compare Istriot puorta, Italian porta, Romanian poartă, Spanish puerta, Friulian puarte.

radaica.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *rādīca, from Latin rādīx. Compare Italian radice, Venetan raixa, Sicilian ràdica, Occitan rasiga.

recanjala.etymology: From a derivative of Latin racana (“upper garment, wrap”).

redro.etymology: From Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre.

rondaina.etymology: From a derivative of Latin hirundo, hirundine. Compare Italian rondine.

ruoma.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *rāma, from Latin rāmus.

sablaun.etymology: From Late Latin sablō, sablōnem, from Latin sabulō, sabulōnem. Compare Romansh sablun, French sablon.

santut.etymology: From Latin sānitās, sānitātem. Compare Italian sanità (archaic santà), Romanian sănătate, French santé, Occitan santat.

sapaun.etymology: From Latin sāpō, sāpōnem. Compare Italian sapone, Romanian săpun, Portuguese sabão.

sapto.etymology: From Latin septem. Compare Romanian șapte, Italian sette.

satoil.etymology: From Latin satullus, diminutive of satur. Compare Romanian sătul (“full, weary”), Italian satollo (“full, replete”), and French saoul (“drunk”).

saupra.etymology: From Latin supra. Compare Italian sopra.

sčela.etymology: From Late Latin astella, from astla, from Latin assula.

sčor.etymology: From Latin obscūrus. Compare Italian scuro.

scutro.etymology: From Latin excutiō. Compare Romanian scoate, compare also Italian scuotere.

secla.etymology: From Latin sīcīlis, sīcīlem. Compare Romanian seceră.

seclur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sicilāre, from Latin sicilis (“sickle”). Compare Friulian seselâ.

secut.etymology: From Latin siccātus, past participle of siccō.

sedarul.etymology: From Latin sūdariōlum (“little handkerchief”), diminutive of sūdārium.

septuanta.etymology: From Latin septuaginta. Compare Italian settanta.

sombreja.etymology: From a derivative of Vulgar Latin *subumbrāre, from Latin sub + umbrāre < umbra. Compare Spanish and Portuguese sombra, Romansch sumbreiva.

spangro.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expingere, from Latin ex- + pangere.

spirač.etymology: From Latin sparagus, asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

sploima.etymology: From metathesis of Vulgar Latin *spūmula, from Latin spūma.

stasaun.etymology: From Latin statiō, statiōnem. Compare Old Italian stazzo, stazzone.

stentur.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin extemptāre, from Latin ex- + temptō, temptāre. Compare Italian stentare.

stotur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *extūtāre, from Latin tūtārī (“avert, ward off”).

sublar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūbilāre, from Latin sībilāre.

sugol.etymology: From a derivative of Latin sūgō (“suck”). Compare Romanian sugar (“suckling”).

surca pizigaun.etymology: From a composite formed from the derivative of Latin sōrex, sōricem (“mouse”).

susana.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *susīna, from Latin Sūsa (“ancient capital of Elam”). Compare Italian susina, susino, Friulian susìn.

taljur.etymology: From Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”).

raigno.etymology: Ultimately from Latin rēgnum. Compare Italian regno.

tragala.etymology: From Latin trāgula. Compare Italian tragula, French traille, Portuguese tralha, trelha, Spanish tralla, traílla, compare also Romanian targă.

glazait.etymology: Probably from Latin glaciātus, past participle of glaciō. Compare Italian ghiacciato, Romanian înghețat, French glacé, Friulian glačât.

uaclo.etymology: From Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus.

vaple.etymology: From Latin opulus. Compare Italian loppio, oppio.

uapto.etymology: From Latin octō. Compare Romanian opt, Italian otto, French huit, Spanish ocho, Romansh otg, Occitan uèch, Megleno-Romanian uopt.

vuarb.etymology: From Latin orbus. Compare Friulian vuarb, Istriot uorbo, Romanian orb, Venetan and Italian orbo. Compare also Albanian verbër.

vuarz.etymology: From Latin hordeum. Compare Friulian vuardi, Romanian orz, Italian orzo.

vuas.etymology: From Latin ossum, popular variant of os. Compare Friulian vues, Spanish hueso, Italian osso, Romanian os, Megleno-Romanian uos, Romansh ies.

vaila.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *vēla, from the plural of Latin vēlum.

vaita.etymology:
From Latin vītis f.
Compare Istriot veîda, Romanian viță, Venetan vida, Italian vite.

viala.etymology: From Latin viverrula, diminutive of viverra.

viant.etymology: From Latin ventus. Compare Italian vento, Romanian vânt, Spanish viento, Romansh vent, Friulian vint.

vičain.etymology: From Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

vieclo.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

ziziul.etymology: From Late Latin digitāle, from Latin digitālis.

cotidiun.etymology: Borrowed from Latin cotidianus; compare Italian quotidiano.

santificuot.etymology: From Latin sānctificātus; compare Italian santificato.

sostuanza.etymology: From Latin substantia; compare Italian sostanza.

malamiant.etymology: From mal + -miant < Latin mente. Compare Italian malamente.

junkaura.etymology: From Vulgar Latin ad (h)anc (h)ora(m), from Latin ad hanc hōram "at this hour". Compare Italian ancora, French encore.

ruzuda.etymology: Borrowed from a neighbouring language, e.g. Istriot ruzàda, from Vulgar Latin *rōsāta. Compare Italian rugiada.

subatu.etymology: From Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (šabbāṯ, “Sabbath”).

usur.etymology: From Latin ūsus, past participle of utor.

jocur.etymology: From Latin jocare (“to joke, to play”). Compare Italian giocare, Spanish jugar.

coresma.etymology: From Latin quadragesima, likely borrowed from another Romance language.

anera.etymology: From an older form *anedra (with later assimilation of /dr/ to /rr/), derived from Vulgar Latin *anatria, from Latin anatem. Compare Italian anatra, Istriot ànera, Venetan ànara and others.

botičél.etymology: From a diminutive of Latin buttis (cf. the suffix -cellus).

pesaint.etymology: From Latin pēnsāns, present participle of pēnsō. Compare Italian pesante. Doublet of pesunt.

setemúna.etymology: From Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”).

niar.etymology: Borrowed from Venetan, from Latin nigrum.

vetrun.etymology: From Latin veterānus, probably through the syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form vetrānus. Compare Old Venetan vetrano, Friulian vedran, Romanian bătrân.

muosclo.etymology: From Vulgar Latin masclus, from Latin masculus.

suang.etymology: From Latin sanguis, through a Vulgar Latin sanguem.

puoscua.etymology: From Vulgar Latin pascua, from Latin pascha, from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha, “Passover”). Compare Italian pasqua.

suart.etymology: From Latin sors, sortem. Compare Istriot suorto, Italian sorte, Romanian soartă, Spanish suerte.

jaun.etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis. Compare Venetan xovane.

roita.etymology: From Latin rūta, from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).

infiarn.etymology: From Latin īnfernus, īnfernum. Compare Istriot infierno.

marcus.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *(a)māricōsus, from Latin amārus. Compare Spanish and Portuguese amargoso, Sardinian marigosu.

octuanta.etymology: From Latin octāgintā; this form was probably not inherited but borrowed.

luminur.etymology: From Latin illūmināre, or from lūmināre.

pentaur.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *pinctor, *pinctorem, from Latin pictor.

invelenuot.etymology: From a past participle of a verb derived from Latin venēnum, or from a Vulgar Latin *invenenātus, from Latin venenātus, perfect passive participle of venenō. Compare Venetan invełenà, Romanian înveninat, Italian avvelenato, Spanish envenena

scul.etymology: From Latin axilla, or Late Latin ascella, Vulgar Latin *axella.

castial.etymology: From Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum.

matuos.etymology: From Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa).

caniastro.etymology: From Latin canistrum, from Ancient Greek κάναστρον (kánastron), κάνιστρον (kánistron).

pinsamiant.etymology: From a derivative of Latin pensō + -miant, from Latin -mentum. Compare Catalan pensament, Portuguese pensamento, Spanish pensamiento.

ziant.etymology: From Latin gens, gentem. Compare Istriot zento, Venetan zente, Romanian gint.

zuap.etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin cloppus; compare Italian zoppo, Romanian șchiop, cf. also Occitan and Catalan esclop, Old French clop.

viard.etymology: From Vulgar Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis.

viarz.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *virdia (“cabbage”) (see there for Romance cognates), a substantivization of Vulgar Latin virdis (“green”) (via the neuter plural), syncopated from Classical viridis.

muogro.etymology: From Latin macrum, accusative singular of macer.

nosko.etymology: From non so che (“I don't know what”), from Latin nōn sapiō quid. Compare semantic evolution of Romanian niște, neștine.

siampro.etymology: From Latin semper. Compare Istriot senpro.

sianpro.etymology: From Latin semper. Compare Istriot senpro.

racuardar.etymology: From Latin recordārī. Compare Istriot racurdà.

glosses_en: to stay up, keep a vigil
vejur.etymology: From Latin vigilāre; cf. Italian vegliare.

vedoit.etymology: Past participle of vedar, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *vidūtus in place of Latin vīsus. Compare Italian veduto, Romanian văzut, French vu.

suars.etymology: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin sor(p)sum, from Latin sorbitum, supine of sorbeō. Compare Italian sorso.

medesem.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from Latin -met + ipse + -issimus. Compare Italian medesimo.

stiass.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *st + ipsu, contraction of Latin istum ipsum. Compare Italian stesso, Venetan steso, stes, Friulian stes, istès.

jacqua.etymology: From Latin aqua from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂. Compare Italian acqua and Sicilian jacqua.

lebro.etymology: From Latin liber, librum (“book”). Compare Istriot leîbro, Italian libro.

serur.etymology: From Late Latin serāre, from Latin sera (“bolt, crossbar”).

glosses_en: a diminutive of the male given name Antune, equivalent to English Tony

sinjaur.etymology: From Latin senior. Compare Italian signore, Spanish señor, Portuguese senhor, and French seigneur.

comprur.etymology: Probably from Latin comparare (“to gather, to purchase”). Compare Italian comprare, Spanish comprar.

seraul.etymology: From Latin soror. Compare Italian sorella.

suald.etymology: From Latin solidus. Compare Italian soldo.

sualdi.etymology: From Latin solidus. Compare Italian soldo.

perké.etymology: From Latin per + quid; cf. Italian perché.

paraul.etymology: From Latin parabola. Compare Italian parola.

favlur.etymology: Either from Late Latin fābellāri or Latin fābulārī.

restur.etymology: From Latin restāre. Compare Italian restare.

inserur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *inserāre (“to include, enclose”), from Late Latin serāre, from Latin sera.

gomitur.etymology: From Latin vomitāre, frequentative of vomō (“spew”). Compare Venetan gomitar, Friulian gomitâ, dialectal Portuguese gomitar.

glosses_en: to level, make flat (e.g. the ground/earth)
gualisur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *aequalisāre, from Latin aequālis.

reticuot.etymology: From Medieval Latin hereticus, possibly through Italian eretico, with a past participle ending added. Ultimately from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós).

inparur.etymology: From Latin imparare (“to prepare in”). Compare Italian imparare.

glosses_en: Vegliot (the dialect of Dalmatian spoken in Veglia)

nuot.etymology: From Latin noctem, accusative of nox, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Compare Istriot nuoto, Italian notte, Romanian noapte, Venetan note, Romansh not.

moduonde.etymology: From Latin mutandus (“which is to be changed”). Compare Italian mutande, Venetan mudande.

paiš.etymology: From Latin pagus (“district, countryside”). Compare Italian paese, Spanish país.

fruot.etymology: From Latin fructus (“fruit”). Compare Italian frutto, Spanish fruta.

amazur.etymology: From Latin mactare (“to sacrifice, to kill”). Compare Italian ammazzare.

travalur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tripaliāre (“to work”). Compare Spanish trabajar.

imprendro.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, from Latin prehendere.

prendro.etymology: From Latin prendere, alternative form of prehendere.

incaricur.etymology: From Latin in + carricāre. Compare Romanian încărca.

dicro.etymology: From Latin dīcere, present active participle of dīcō.

parlur.etymology: From Latin parabolō. Compare French parler, Italian parlare, Portuguese parlar, Spanish parlar.

caricur.etymology: From Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus. Compare French charger, Italian caricare, Portuguese carregar, and Spanish cargar.

castrur.etymology: From Latin castrāre. Compare French castrer, Italian castrare, Portuguese castrar, and Spanish castrar.

odiur.etymology: From Latin odiō. Compare Italian odiare, Portuguese odiar, and Spanish odiar.

vular.etymology: From Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

legro.etymology: From Latin legere, from Latin legō.

scribro.etymology: From Latin scribere, from Latin scribō.

lasčur.etymology: From Latin laxāre, from Latin laxō.

ponro.etymology: From Latin ponere, from Latin ponō.

elegro.etymology: From Latin eligere, from Latin eligō.

inizur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin initiāre, from Latin initium.

despoliur.etymology: From Latin dēspoliāre. Compare Italian spogliare, Romanian despuia, French dépouiller, Occitan despolhar, Spanish despojar.

glosses_en: to exile, banish, send away, cast out
esiliur.etymology: From Latin exiliāre. Compare Italian esiliare.

vendro.etymology: From Latin vēndō. Compare Catalan, Occitan, and French vendre.

advocur.etymology: Borrowed from Latin advocāre. Compare Italian advocare.

glosses_en: To get underway and pick up speed.

provocur.etymology: Borrowed from Latin provocāre. Compare Italian provocare.

provur.etymology: From Latin probāre. Compare Italian provare.

comprensiaun.etymology: Borrowed from Italian comprensione, from Latin comprehēnsiō.

aprendro.etymology: From Latin apprendere, alternative form of apprehendere.

colegro.etymology: From Latin colligere, from Latin colligō.

afacro.etymology: Cf. Italian affare, French affaire, Spanish afer.

abucur.etymology: From Latin advocāre. Compare Italian advocare.

comanduar.etymology: From Late Latin commandāre, from Latin commendāre.

grabia.etymology: From a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *grabji.

carituat.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cāritās, cāritātem, probably borrowed from Italian carità.

furmiant.etymology: From Latin frumentum, from fruor (“to use, enjoy”) + -mentum (instrumental suffix).

glosses_en: first-person plural indicative future/conditional of zer
second-person plural indicative future/conditional of zer

respondro.etymology: From Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.

affuor.etymology: a (“to”) + fuor (“to do”). Compare Italian affare, French affaire.

altramiante.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente.

anduar.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin. Possibly from *ambitāre (literally “go around”), frequentative of ambiō. Alternatively, perhaps from an earlier *amnāre < *amlāre < ambulāre (“walk”), or from Celtic root mn-

glosses_en: a male given name from Latin, equivalent to English Anthony
a diminutive of the male given name Antune, equivalent to English Tony

argust.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin lacusta; compare Italian aragosta.

glosses_en: Vrbnik (a village and municipality on the east coast of Krk, Croatia)

loine.etymology: From Latin Lunae dīēs, variant of dīēs Lunae.

crobolo.etymology: From Late Latin cribellum, diminutive of Latin cribrum.

cociaina.etymology: From Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna, ultimately from Latin coquō (“cook”, verb).

iarba.etymology: From Latin herba. Compare Romanian iarbă, Italian erba, Spanish hierba.

uars.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos
Proto-Italic *orsos
Latin ursus
Dalmatian uars
Inherited from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos.

glosses_en: Dalmatia (a historical region of Croatia, on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea)
Dalmatia (a province of the Roman Empire)
Dalmátia.etymology: From an Illyrian tribe called the Dalmatae who lived in the region. Believed to be borrowed from Illyrian, akin to Albanian delmë, dele (“sheep”). The toponym Delminium has the same origin.

regaina.etymology: Inherited from Latin rēgīna; cognate with Italian regina and Spanish reina.

iacqua.etymology: From Latin aqua from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂. Compare Italian acqua.

insuain.etymology: From Latin somnium. Compare Italian sogno.

siapto.etymology: From Latin septem. Compare Romanian șapte, Italian sette.

libertut.etymology: From Latin lībertās, lībertātem; compare Italian libertà.

puritut.etymology: From Late Latin pūritās, pūritātem, from Latin pūrus.

i/languages A to L.etymology: From Latin illī, nominative masculine plural of ille. Compare Italian i, gli.
